06Equipment Uptime, Recipes, and Tool MatchingSame recipe, different means+

Your goal

Distinguish recipe identity, specification performance, tool matching, and equipment availability in a transfer discussion.

This lesson in the book, page 49 ↗

A Read the situation

Same recipe, different means

Equipment engineer Victor and process engineer Asha compare tools A and B using the same identified R7 recipe and an agreed comparable measurement basis. Their film-thickness sample means are 98 nm and 102 nm. The local mean specification is 95 to 105 nm, but the tool-matching criterion requires the means to differ by no more than 2 nm. Tool B was available for 900 of a defined 1,000-minute window. A colleague uses the identical recipe and 90% availability to claim B is an approved interchangeable backup. No transfer approval is recorded.

Victor: Equipment engineer / Asha: Process engineer

Check the facts · 3 questions

Choose the answer supported by the briefing. Do not assume that a proposed action has already happened.

1. How far apart are the sample means?

Answer and explanation

D. 4 nm

The difference between 102 nm and 98 nm is four nanometers.

2. Do the means meet the stated matching criterion?

Answer and explanation

C. No; 4 nm exceeds the allowed 2 nm difference.

The matching criterion applies to the difference between means, not merely each mean's specification status.

3. What does 90% describe here?

Answer and explanation

A. Availability for 900 of the defined 1,000 minutes

The supplied time ratio concerns equipment availability and establishes no product-yield or approval claim.

B Find the words

Vocabulary and collocations

Both sample means meet the local 95-to-105 nm mean specification. Their difference is 4 nm, so they fail the separate 2 nm matching criterion. This does not establish the status of every individual wafer, whose measurements are not supplied.

24 field terms and natural word combinations
tool matching
Demonstrating comparable tool performance against defined criteria.assess tool matching
chamber matching
Demonstrating comparable performance between process chambers.verify chamber matching
recipe revision
The identified version of a process recipe.confirm the recipe revision
setpoint
A commanded target value for a controlled variable.record the setpoint
actual value
The measured or achieved value rather than the commanded target.compare setpoint and actual value
equipment state
The recorded operational condition of a tool.report equipment state
availability
The share of a defined time basis during which equipment is available.calculate equipment availability
utilization
The share of a stated time basis during which equipment is used.state the utilization denominator
scheduled downtime
Planned time when equipment is unavailable for the defined use.plan scheduled downtime
unscheduled downtime
Unplanned time when equipment is unavailable.investigate unscheduled downtime
preventive maintenance
Planned work intended to reduce equipment failures or deterioration.schedule preventive maintenance
corrective maintenance
Work to restore equipment after a fault or failure.complete corrective maintenance
MTBF
Mean time between failures under a stated operating and event definition.report MTBF
MTTR
Mean time to repair or restore under the stated local definition.define the MTTR basis
chamber condition
The physical and operating state of a process chamber.assess chamber condition
seasoning
Controlled processing used to establish a required chamber condition.verify seasoning status
calibration status
The current documented state of required measurement calibration.check calibration status
qualification wafer
A wafer used to assess a specified tool or process condition.evaluate a qualification wafer
monitor wafer
A wafer used to track selected process or tool behavior.review monitor-wafer results
matching criterion
A defined limit for acceptable performance difference.apply the matching criterion
process transfer
Moving a defined process to another tool or location.approve process transfer
backup tool
An alternative tool intended for use under defined conditions.qualify a backup tool
release status
Whether the required authorization for a specified use is in place.confirm release status
offset correction
A controlled adjustment addressing a measured systematic difference.assess offset correction

Availability is 900 divided by 1,000, or 90%, on this stated basis. It does not measure process matching, output yield, or production-use approval. Availability and utilization definitions vary, so keep the time denominator explicit.

C Notice the language

Name which readiness question you answered

Available, in specification, matched, and released describe different conditions. A tool may satisfy one and not another. Give each claim its own evidence and criterion so production planning does not convert equipment uptime into process-transfer approval.

16 useful phrases, grouped by purpose
Confirm the recipe
Both tools used the identified R7 revision.
Separate inputs from outputs
Identical setpoints do not prove identical performance.
State the means
A measured 98 nm and B measured 102 nm.
Give the difference
The means are 4 nm apart.
Apply the right criterion
Matching allows no more than a 2 nm difference.
Separate the specifications
Both means are in spec, but the pair is not matched.
Bound the evidence
These are sample means, not every individual wafer result.
Ask about chamber state
Were the relevant chamber conditions documented?
Check measurement status
Confirm the calibration and measurement basis.
State availability
B was available for 900 of the defined 1,000 minutes.
Keep the percentage limited
That 90% figure is availability, not yield.
Avoid automatic substitution
Backup status needs the required qualification and approval.
Route the investigation
Review the observed offset before proposing a correction.
Preserve authorization
Do not change the recipe from this comparison alone.
Clarify the transfer
Which process, product, and tool combination is proposed?
Close the status
Report specification, matching, availability, and release separately.
6 language and precision notes
Same
Identify whether recipe, settings, product, or measured outcome is the same.
Available
Describes a time or operational state, not qualification.
In spec
Specify the metric; a passing mean does not prove every unit passed.
Matched
Requires an actual matching criterion and supporting evidence.
Backup
A planning role that does not automatically authorize production use.
Offset
A measured difference to investigate, not an instruction to adjust settings.

D Check your understanding

Choose the precise message

Choose one best answer using the case facts and the stated purpose.

1. Which status report is accurate?

Answer and explanation

C. Both means meet the mean specification; their 4 nm difference fails the 2 nm matching limit.

The specification and matching tests use different criteria, and individual results are not supplied.

2. What does using the same recipe establish?

Answer and explanation

B. The identified recipe input is shared, not that output performance is interchangeable.

Shared commanded inputs do not establish identical physical conditions, equivalent output, or authorization to transfer the process.

3. Which calculation matches the availability basis?

Answer and explanation

C. 900 divided by 1,000 equals 90%.

Availability is available time over the defined window. Ten percent is the unavailable fraction, and utilization needs its own use-time data and basis.

4. What remains necessary before calling B an approved interchangeable backup?

Answer and explanation

B. The required matching or qualification evidence and transfer approval

The case lacks matching acceptance and transfer approval, neither of which is replaced by uptime.

Check explanations in the book, page 95 ↗

E Conversations

Same recipe, different means

Extended conversation · 20 turns · 10 gaps

Victor: Equipment engineer / Asha: Process engineer

Complete the numbered gaps. Use each bank entry once, without changing its form.

Word bank
  • matching criterion
  • chamber condition
  • calibration status
  • process transfer
  • Tool matching
  • equipment state
  • release status
  • actual value
  • availability
  • recipe revision
  1. Victor
    Tool B has the same R7 recipe as A and was available for ninety percent of the window. The planning note calls it an interchangeable backup.
  2. Asha
    That combines different questions. 1 depends on the measured outcomes and our criterion, not only the recipe name or the amount of time the tool was available.
  3. Victor
    We confirmed the same recipe revision and an agreed measurement basis. A's sample mean was ninety-eight nanometers, while B's was one hundred two.
  4. Asha
    The 2 allows a difference of no more than two nanometers. These means differ by four, so this comparison does not establish an acceptable match.
  5. Victor
    Both means are within the local mean specification of ninety-five to one hundred five. That explains why someone thought the comparison had passed.
  6. Asha
    The 3 has to be assessed against the correct question. Each mean passes that specification, but the pair fails the separate matching limit.
  7. Victor
    I will say both sample means meet that limit. We have not reviewed every individual measurement, so I cannot extend that claim to every wafer.
  8. Asha
    Agreed. Confirm the 4 and report the evidence at its actual level. Do not let a summary mean or a shared input become a claim about every processed unit.
  9. Victor
    The observed difference needs investigation. Chamber history and maintenance condition may be relevant, but neither has been established as the cause from these numbers.
  10. Asha
    Review 5 and the other appropriate records. Identical commanded settings do not guarantee identical physical conditions or measurement behavior.
  11. Victor
    I will bring the calibration and monitor records. Can we review those before anyone suggests changing R7 to remove the offset?
  12. Asha
    Check 6 through the approved process. We should not prescribe a recipe adjustment before the team understands the relevant evidence and authorization requirements.
  13. Victor
    For the uptime figure, B was available for nine hundred minutes out of a defined one-thousand-minute window. That calculation gives ninety percent.
  14. Asha
    Label it 7 and retain the denominator. It does not mean ninety percent yield or ninety percent confidence that the tool can substitute for A.
  15. Victor
    We also have no usage-time figure here, so we should not relabel availability as utilization. The two measures can use different time bases and answer different questions.
  16. Asha
    Correct. The 8 record helps explain the time measure, but an available tool is not automatically qualified for this product and process combination.
  17. Victor
    The backup proposal remains useful because capacity is constrained, but it needs the appropriate technical assessment and approval before production relies on it.
  18. Asha
    Treat it as a 9 decision. The defined scope, matching evidence, and required authorization must be clear instead of being inferred from the existence of an alternative tool.
  19. Victor
    I will revise the planning note to separate the passing means, failed matching comparison, ninety-percent availability, and missing approval. It will no longer call B interchangeable.
  20. Asha
    That preserves the 10 accurately. We can pursue the backup option while making its unresolved requirements visible to the people planning production.

Answers and explanations
  1. Tool matching Turn 2. Tool matching requires measured performance against a defined comparison criterion, not simply a shared recipe or uptime figure.
  2. matching criterion Turn 4. The matching criterion allows no more than two nanometers between means; the observed difference is four.
  3. actual value Turn 6. Actual value concerns the measured outcome; passing the mean specification does not remove the separate difference between tools.
  4. recipe revision Turn 8. The recipe revision identifies the shared controlled input, but cannot stand in for unsupplied individual wafer evidence.
  5. chamber condition Turn 10. Chamber condition is a possible contributor to tool behavior that must be assessed rather than assumed from the recipe.
  6. calibration status Turn 12. Calibration status concerns the documented measurement basis and is relevant to interpreting the observed tool difference.
  7. availability Turn 14. Availability is the available-time fraction on the stated basis, not a measure of matching, yield, or approval.
  8. equipment state Turn 16. Equipment state records the tool's operational condition; an available state does not establish qualified process performance.
  9. process transfer Turn 18. Process transfer moves a defined process to another tool and requires its own relevant assessment and approval.
  10. release status Turn 20. Release status records authorization for the intended use, which remains absent despite the tool's availability and passing means.

  13. Victor: For the uptime figure, B was available for nine hundred minutes out of a defined one-thousand-minute window. That calculation gives ninety percent.
  14. Asha: Label it availability and retain the denominator. It does not mean ninety percent yield or ninety percent confidence that the tool can substitute for A.
  15. Victor: We also have no usage-time figure here, so we should not relabel availability as utilization. The two measures can use different time bases and answer different questions.
  16. Asha: Correct. The equipment state record helps explain the time measure, but an available tool is not automatically qualified for this product and process combination.
  17. Victor: The backup proposal remains useful because capacity is constrained, but it needs the appropriate technical assessment and approval before production relies on it.
  18. Asha: Treat it as a process transfer decision. The defined scope, matching evidence, and required authorization must be clear instead of being inferred from the existence of an alternative tool.
  19. Victor: I will revise the planning note to separate the passing means, failed matching comparison, ninety-percent availability, and missing approval. It will no longer call B interchangeable.
  20. Asha: That preserves the release status accurately. We can pursue the backup option while making its unresolved requirements visible to the people planning production.
Dialogue in the book, page 55 ↗
Three more conversations at work

Each short conversation has its own fictional situation and facts.

The same recipe name does not establish tool matching

Fictional equipment comparison using the lesson case: two tools run the same nominal recipe but produce different measured results.

  1. Production planner: Both tools run the same nominal recipe. Can we treat their output as interchangeable?
  2. Equipment engineer: The measured results differ, so the shared recipe name doesn't establish tool matching.
  3. Production planner: What should we compare before choosing which tool to allocate to the next evaluation?
  4. Equipment engineer: Use comparable product, measurement conditions, configuration records, and relevant maintenance history for both tools.
  5. Production planner: Tool A has better uptime. Would that alone make it the stronger option?
  6. Equipment engineer: It helps availability, but uptime doesn't answer whether the process results meet the same requirements.
  7. Production planner: So the tradeoff may involve availability and demonstrated process performance, not a single winner.
  8. Equipment engineer: Exactly. We should also distinguish measured differences from any unverified explanation about their cause.
  9. Production planner: I'll request a like-for-like comparison and avoid assigning work based only on the recipe label.
  10. Equipment engineer: I'll bring the tool-matching evidence and open questions to the responsible allocation review.
Uptime measured with different exclusions

Fictional equipment report: one tool's uptime excludes preventive-maintenance hours, while another report includes those hours in its denominator.

  1. Operations manager: Tool A's uptime is higher than tool B's. Should we prioritize A for capacity planning?
  2. Equipment analyst: Their reports treat preventive maintenance differently, so the percentages aren't directly comparable yet.
  3. Operations manager: Can you explain the mismatch without getting lost in the dashboard calculation details?
  4. Equipment analyst: One percentage excludes planned maintenance time; the other includes it in the time being measured.
  5. Operations manager: Then we need the same measurement boundary before ranking their availability from those figures.
  6. Equipment analyst: Yes. I'll recalculate using an agreed definition and show planned maintenance separately.
  7. Operations manager: Will that establish which tool produces better process results or meets matching requirements?
  8. Equipment analyst: No. Availability and process performance are separate criteria, and both matter to the allocation discussion.
  9. Operations manager: Please bring the aligned uptime view together with the existing process-performance evidence.
  10. Equipment analyst: I will, with unknown matching status visible rather than concealed behind a favorable availability figure.
A maintained tool versus an unreviewed backup

Fictional scheduling review: tool A has completed preventive maintenance but awaits post-maintenance review; backup tool B is available but matching status is unknown.

  1. Scheduling lead: Tool A's maintenance is finished. Should we use it immediately instead of the available backup?
  2. Equipment engineer: Maintenance completion is recorded, but the post-maintenance review is pending. Availability alone doesn't establish readiness.
  3. Scheduling lead: Tool B is available now. Does its backup designation mean tool matching is already confirmed?
  4. Equipment engineer: Not in the records we have. Its matching status is unknown and needs owner confirmation.
  5. Scheduling lead: Then both choices have open conditions, although their reasons are different.
  6. Equipment engineer: Correct. Compare readiness evidence, scheduling availability, and product suitability on the same basis.
  7. Scheduling lead: Can we propose A subject to review while requesting B's matching record as an alternative?
  8. Equipment engineer: We can take those conditional options to the authorized planning owner without directing an unapproved run.
  9. Scheduling lead: I'll keep maintenance complete, readiness pending, and backup matching unknown as separate status entries.
  10. Equipment engineer: That makes the tradeoff transparent and avoids treating either tool as qualified by assumption.

F Say it

Two scenarios to practice

Same recipe, different means
  1. Check the answers. Read the 98 nm and 102 nm means, then the separate specification and matching limits.
  2. Switch roles. Read the availability exchange without replacing availability with yield or utilization.

On your own: read both roles. With a partner: swap roles after the first reading. Use the completed conversation to check any line you need to repeat.

Two different limits

Two tools have sample means of 50 and 53 nm. Both meet a mean specification of 48 to 55 nm. Matching allows at most 1 nm difference. Transfer approval is pending.

Choose one reply for each gap, then read the four turns in order. Check the explanation after each choice.

1. Engineer: "Both means meet the 48-to-55 nm ___."

Answer and explanation

D. specification

The specification applies to each sample mean, and both 50 and 53 fall within it.

2. Reviewer: "But their three-nanometer gap misses our one-nanometer ___."

Answer and explanation

A. matching criterion

The matching criterion applies to the three-nanometer difference, which exceeds the permitted one.

3. Engineer: "Then moving this process to the other tool remains a proposed ___."

Answer and explanation

A. process transfer

Process transfer is the move between tools and requires its own assessment and authorization.

4. Reviewer: "Correct. Keep approval pending in the ___ field."

Answer and explanation

A. release status

Release status concerns authorization; passing individual means does not establish that approval.

Read the completed exchange twice, switching roles. Keep the printed facts and professional responsibilities unchanged.

Lesson 06: Equipment Uptime, Recipes, and Tool Matching
Original fictional case: Equipment engineer Victor and process engineer Asha compare tools A and B using the same identified R7 recipe and an agreed comparable measurement basis. Their film-thickness sample means are 98 nm and 102 nm. The local mean specification is 95 to 105 nm, but the tool-matching criterion requires the means to differ by no more than 2 nm. Tool B was available for 900 of a defined 1,000-minute window. A colleague uses the identical recipe and 90% availability to claim B is an approved interchangeable backup. No transfer approval is recorded.
Language workshop: Same recipe, different means
Communication goal: Distinguish recipe identity, specification performance, tool matching, and equipment availability in a transfer discussion.
Language guidance: Both sample means meet the local 95-to-105 nm mean specification. Their difference is 4 nm, so they fail the separate 2 nm matching criterion. This does not establish the status of every individual wafer, whose measurements are not supplied.
Useful expressions (preserve the supplied facts): Both tools used the identified R7 revision. / Identical setpoints do not prove identical performance. / A measured 98 nm and B measured 102 nm. / The means are 4 nm apart. / Matching allows no more than a 2 nm difference. / Both means are in spec, but the pair is not matched. / These are sample means, not every individual wafer result. / Were the relevant chamber conditions documented? / Confirm the calibration and measurement basis. / B was available for 900 of the defined 1,000 minutes. / That 90% figure is availability, not yield. / Backup status needs the required qualification and approval. / Review the observed offset before proposing a correction. / Do not change the recipe from this comparison alone. / Which process, product, and tool combination is proposed? / Report specification, matching, availability, and release separately.
Vocabulary: tool matching: Demonstrating comparable tool performance against defined criteria. / chamber matching: Demonstrating comparable performance between process chambers. / recipe revision: The identified version of a process recipe. / setpoint: A commanded target value for a controlled variable. / actual value: The measured or achieved value rather than the commanded target. / equipment state: The recorded operational condition of a tool. / availability: The share of a defined time basis during which equipment is available. / utilization: The share of a stated time basis during which equipment is used. / scheduled downtime: Planned time when equipment is unavailable for the defined use. / unscheduled downtime: Unplanned time when equipment is unavailable. / preventive maintenance: Planned work intended to reduce equipment failures or deterioration. / corrective maintenance: Work to restore equipment after a fault or failure. / MTBF: Mean time between failures under a stated operating and event definition. / MTTR: Mean time to repair or restore under the stated local definition. / chamber condition: The physical and operating state of a process chamber. / seasoning: Controlled processing used to establish a required chamber condition. / calibration status: The current documented state of required measurement calibration. / qualification wafer: A wafer used to assess a specified tool or process condition. / monitor wafer: A wafer used to track selected process or tool behavior. / matching criterion: A defined limit for acceptable performance difference. / process transfer: Moving a defined process to another tool or location. / backup tool: An alternative tool intended for use under defined conditions. / release status: Whether the required authorization for a specified use is in place. / offset correction: A controlled adjustment addressing a measured systematic difference.
Speaking task: Check the answers. Read the 98 nm and 102 nm means, then the separate specification and matching limits. Switch roles. Read the availability exchange without replacing availability with yield or utilization. Complete and check the transfer. Read each claim with its own criterion and keep approval pending.
Partner: Victor: Equipment engineer / Asha: Process engineer
Guided response task: Select supplied answers for the dialogue gaps. Check the explanations, then read the completed exchange aloud; no original writing is required.
Optional second-round challenge: Two tools have sample means of 50 and 53 nm. Both meet a mean specification of 48 to 55 nm. Matching allows at most 1 nm difference. Transfer approval is pending.

Asha: Treat it as a process transfer decision. The defined scope, matching evidence, and required authorization must be clear instead of being inferred from the existence of an alternative tool.
Victor: I will revise the planning note to separate the passing means, failed matching comparison, ninety-percent availability, and missing approval. It will no longer call B interchangeable.
Asha: That preserves the release status accurately. We can pursue the backup option while making its unresolved requirements visible to the people planning production.

TASK: Interactive workplace role-play
1. Use the supplied case or dialogue as the starting situation. Give a two-sentence briefing and offer two relevant professional roles for me to choose from. For a supplied dialogue, use its actual roles. Ask which role I want, then stop and wait. Do not write my replies.
2. After I choose, identify who you will play and the immediate communication goal. Play the other professional; where a meeting requires a third person, label each of your speakers clearly. Start with one natural workplace turn and wait for my reply. Keep most turns to one to three sentences and ask no more than one question at a time.
3. Let the exchange develop across six to ten learner turns, or end earlier if I type "feedback". Respond to what I actually say. Include a plausible clarification, disagreement or tradeoff without silently changing the starting facts. Mark any added constraint as a fictional second-round variation. Do not resolve approvals, evidence or commitments that remain uncertain.
4. Stay in role during the exchange. If my meaning is unclear, ask for clarification naturally. Give a hint only if I ask or cannot proceed. Do not deliver a model conversation in advance.
5. At the debrief, quote two of my phrases: one successful choice and one worth improving. Check factual accuracy, language, register and whether the next step was clear. Give up to three focused suggestions. Ask me to retry the weakest turn; wait. Only then offer an alternative wording and a harder replay.
Use voice replies when available. If I prefer selections, offer four plausible spoken replies and explain my choice before continuing. Do not require written compositions.

07Packaging, Test, and Reliability QualificationOne completed test is not complete qualification+

Your goal

Explain qualification status test by test, preserve configuration scope, and correct an overbroad customer claim.

This lesson in the book, page 58 ↗

A Read the situation

One completed test is not complete qualification

Product engineer Diego and reliability engineer Mei review package Q7. Its approved fictional qualification plan requires temperature cycling, high-temperature operating life testing, a highly accelerated stress test, and final review of the evidence. Temperature cycling has passed under its protocol. Operating-life testing is running, and the accelerated stress test has not started. No final approval or accepted substitution is recorded. A customer slide nevertheless says qualification complete. The team must replace that headline with a precise status without describing open tests as failures.

Diego: Product engineer / Mei: Reliability engineer

Check the facts · 3 questions

Choose the answer supported by the briefing. Do not assume that a proposed action has already happened.

1. Which test has passed?

Answer and explanation

A. Temperature cycling

The briefing identifies temperature cycling as the only completed passing test.

2. What is the operating-life test status?

Answer and explanation

A. Running

The supplied plan still includes the test, and its stated status is running.

3. Why is qualification complete unsupported?

Answer and explanation

D. Two required tests and final review remain open.

The defined plan requires evidence and final review that have not all been completed.

B Find the words

Vocabulary and collocations

This case uses a specific fictional plan, not a universal mandatory three-test list. One passing test supports its defined result. It does not complete the two open tests or the final review, and it does not establish every application-specific reliability claim.

24 field terms and natural word combinations
package substrate
The package structure carrying connections between die and external interfaces.specify the package substrate
wire bonding
Forming electrical connections using fine wires.qualify wire bonding
flip-chip attachment
Connecting a die face-down through conductive bumps or pillars.evaluate flip-chip attachment
underfill
Material placed around interconnections to support a package assembly.assess underfill integrity
mold compound
Encapsulating material used in many semiconductor packages.qualify the mold compound
solder joint
A soldered electrical and mechanical connection.inspect solder joints
BGA
Ball grid array, a package connection format using an array of solder balls.assess BGA assembly
QFN
Quad flat no-lead, a package format with exposed connection lands.review the QFN package
SiP
System in package, integrating multiple functions or components in one package.evaluate a SiP design
TSV
Through-silicon via, a conductive connection passing through silicon.characterize TSV connections
package construction
The materials and structural arrangement of a package.identify package construction
moisture sensitivity
Susceptibility to moisture-related effects under stated handling or stress conditions.assess moisture sensitivity
delamination
Separation between bonded material layers.inspect for delamination
thermal cycling
Repeated temperature changes under a specified test profile.complete thermal cycling
HTOL
High-temperature operating life, an operating stress test under defined conditions.report HTOL status
HAST
Highly accelerated stress test, a defined accelerated humidity-related stress test.schedule HAST
preconditioning
Defined preparation before a test to represent relevant handling or assembly stresses.document preconditioning
qualification plan
The defined tests, evidence, scope, and approval requirements for qualification.follow the qualification plan
qualification vehicle
The selected device or structure used to support qualification evidence.identify the qualification vehicle
test coverage
The requirements or failure concerns addressed by the performed tests.assess qualification test coverage
failure analysis
Investigation of failed samples and their causes.initiate failure analysis
qualification by similarity
Use of justified related evidence under an accepted qualification approach.assess qualification by similarity
final test
Electrical testing at the defined final product stage.complete final test
qualification approval
Authorized acceptance of the required qualification evidence.obtain qualification approval

Related package evidence may sometimes support qualification through an accepted similarity rationale. No such substitution is accepted here. Similar appearance, a shared package name, or a convenient schedule cannot silently change the approved evidence requirements.

C Notice the language

Give progress without collapsing the plan

A customer may prefer a short headline, but complete must refer to the required plan and configuration. Name the finished test, the open work, and the pending decision. Do not imply that a test still running has passed, or that a test not yet started has failed.

16 useful phrases, grouped by purpose
Name the completed result
Q7 passed temperature cycling under the stated protocol.
State ongoing work
HTOL is still running.
State unstarted work
HAST has not started.
Keep the plan visible
The approved plan requires all three tests and final review.
Correct the headline
Qualification is in progress, not complete.
Avoid treating pending as failed
No result is available for the unstarted test.
Preserve configuration
Which package construction does the evidence cover?
Ask about the vehicle
Is this the approved qualification vehicle?
Check preparation
Are the required preconditioning records included?
Separate production test
Final test is not a substitute for every reliability stress.
Qualify related evidence
Similarity needs an accepted technical rationale.
Avoid a schedule shortcut
A desired customer date does not remove a required test.
State the approval gap
Final qualification approval is not recorded.
Describe coverage
Identify what each completed test actually addresses.
Commit to the next update
The next report will distinguish completed, running, and unstarted tests.
Close accurately
Keep release decisions with the authorized review process.
6 language and precision notes
Qualified
Specify product, package, construction, scope, and approval.
Passed
Applies to a defined test result, not automatically the entire plan.
Running
A current activity status, not a completed result.
Not started
Does not mean failed or waived.
Similar
Needs a justified and accepted relevance argument.
Complete
Includes the required evidence review, not only laboratory scheduling.

D Check your understanding

Choose the precise message

Choose one best answer using the case facts and the stated purpose.

1. Which customer headline is supported?

Answer and explanation

D. Qualification in progress: temperature cycling passed; HTOL running; HAST not started.

The headline accurately separates each test's status without inventing a result or approval.

2. What does the passing temperature-cycle result establish?

Answer and explanation

D. The stated test result under its protocol and scope

Temperature cycling, operating-life testing, and humidity-related stress address different test conditions. A shared name also does not establish equivalent package construction or scope.

3. When could related evidence replace a required test in this case?

Answer and explanation

D. Only through the applicable accepted change or similarity process, which has not occurred

Related evidence requires an accepted relevance and authorization basis. Dimensions, document age, and a different passing test do not by themselves justify substitution.

4. What should final review examine?

Answer and explanation

A. Required evidence, scope, configuration, open items, and approval conditions

Qualification approval depends on the required evidence and scope, not a favorable summary label.

  1. Diego
    The customer slide says Q7 qualification is complete because temperature cycling passed. We still have two other tests in the plan, so I need a more accurate headline.
  2. Mei
    Start from the 1. Our approved plan requires all three tests and final evidence review. We have completed one part, not the entire qualification decision.
  3. Diego
    The completed test followed its protocol and passed. I want to preserve that positive result rather than make the update sound as though nothing has been achieved.
  4. Mei
    Report the 2 result clearly. Its value is not diminished by stating the other work accurately, and it should not be expanded beyond its protocol and scope.
  5. Diego
    The operating-life test is still running. The lab has not supplied its final result, so the customer should not read the current status as a pass.
  6. Mei
    Label 3 as running. If a progress checkpoint is available, identify it as interim information without treating it as the completed test outcome.
  7. Diego
    The accelerated humidity-related stress test has not started. That is a schedule and evidence gap, but it is not a failed result.
  8. Mei
    Exactly. 4 remains unstarted in this plan. Use that status rather than either a reassuring green result or an unsupported failure label.
  9. Diego
    Which package construction should I name on the slide? Q7 alone may cover variants with different materials or assembly details.
  10. Mei
    Keep the 5 linked to the evidence. Qualification scope should not silently expand to a different variant simply because the marketing name is similar.
  11. Diego
    We should confirm the tested device or structure as well. Otherwise reviewers may not know how the selected samples relate to the configuration being discussed.
  12. Mei
    Identify the 6 and its approved rationale. Traceability makes it possible to review applicability rather than assume that any available sample represents every product.
  13. Diego
    The assembly preparation records also belong in the package. I do not want the final review to discover that important preparation details were omitted from the summary.
  14. Mei
    Include the required 7 records where the plan calls for them. A passing result needs the relevant preparation and test context to be interpreted correctly.
  15. Diego
    Sales wants to reuse results from an older package. I will refer that request for review; we have no accepted substitution for the open tests.
  16. Mei
    8 needs an accepted basis under the applicable process. A related package or a desired delivery date does not automatically change the approved requirements.
  17. Diego
    We also have final electrical test records, but those should not be presented as though they address every stress-related concern in the qualification plan.
  18. Mei
    Correct. 9 differs between production checks and reliability assessments. Each result needs to be connected to what it actually evaluates, not treated as interchangeable evidence.
  19. Diego
    I will change the headline to qualification in progress, list the three statuses, and keep the configuration and outstanding review visible. We will not announce release from this slide.
  20. Mei
    That preserves 10 as a separate decision. The next update can show genuine progress while keeping the unresolved tests and final review clear.

Answers and explanations
  1. qualification plan Turn 2. The qualification plan defines all required tests and final review, so one passing test cannot complete it.
  2. thermal cycling Turn 4. Thermal cycling is the completed temperature-change stress test; its passing result remains valid within its defined protocol.
  3. HTOL Turn 6. HTOL is high-temperature operating life testing, which is currently running rather than completed in this case.
  4. HAST Turn 8. HAST is the highly accelerated stress test that has not started; absence of a result is not a pass or failure.
  5. package construction Turn 10. Package construction identifies the materials and structure covered by the evidence, preventing unsupported extension to other variants.
  6. qualification vehicle Turn 12. The qualification vehicle is the selected device or structure whose results support the defined qualification scope.
  7. preconditioning Turn 14. Preconditioning records show the defined preparation used before testing and form part of interpreting the evidence.
  8. Qualification by similarity Turn 16. Qualification by similarity requires an accepted technical rationale; no such substitution is established in this case.
  9. Test coverage Turn 18. Test coverage identifies which requirements or concerns the available tests address; final electrical testing does not replace every reliability stress.
  10. qualification approval Turn 20. Qualification approval is the authorized acceptance of the required evidence, which remains pending while tests and review are incomplete.

Dialogue in the book, page 64 ↗
Three more conversations at work

Each short conversation has its own fictional situation and facts.

One reliability pass with two tests open

Fictional package review using the lesson case: one reliability test passed, two planned tests remain open, and a slide calls qualification complete.

  1. Customer quality lead: The slide says qualification complete. Have all planned package reliability tests actually finished?
  2. Package engineer: No. One test passed, while two remain open. The completion statement is too broad.
  3. Customer quality lead: Can we preserve the positive result without implying the remaining tests have passed?
  4. Package engineer: Yes. State which test passed and list the two pending tests under their current status.
  5. Customer quality lead: Does an open test mean a failure was found, or simply that its outcome isn't available?
  6. Package engineer: Here it means the planned work is still open; no outcome should be invented.
  7. Customer quality lead: Please also keep electrical binning results separate from the overall reliability qualification claim.
  8. Package engineer: Agreed. Classification by test results doesn't replace evidence for every planned reliability condition.
  9. Customer quality lead: I'll revise the customer wording and ask the qualification owner to confirm the next update.
  10. Package engineer: I'll provide the verified test status and avoid a completion date that hasn't been confirmed.
A burn-in result is not every reliability result

Fictional device review: the recorded burn-in test passed, but the rest of the qualification matrix has not been reviewed in this meeting.

  1. Program manager: The burn-in report passed. Can I summarize that as all reliability requirements being satisfied?
  2. Test engineer: No. That report covers its specified test conditions, not the entire qualification matrix.
  3. Program manager: Could you explain the distinction for colleagues who see burn-in as a complete reliability guarantee?
  4. Test engineer: It is one defined stress-screening or test activity in this program, not proof about every future condition.
  5. Program manager: We haven't reviewed the other reports here, so their status remains unknown to this discussion.
  6. Test engineer: Correct. We should ask the qualification owner for the complete matrix instead of inferring completion.
  7. Program manager: Should I say the remaining tests are failures to prevent anyone assuming they passed?
  8. Test engineer: No. Unknown status is neither a pass nor a failure. Use the actual evidence boundary.
  9. Program manager: I'll report the burn-in result specifically and leave the overall qualification statement pending confirmation.
  10. Test engineer: I'll request the matrix and keep the package configuration attached to the evidence we discuss.
Different bins do not explain the cause

Fictional final-test review: a package lot has more units in a lower performance bin than a reference lot; test-condition comparability is unverified.

  1. Product engineer: More units entered the lower performance bin. Does that prove packaging damaged the devices?
  2. Test analyst: The binning distribution changed, but that observation alone doesn't establish the cause.
  3. Product engineer: What context do we need before interpreting the difference between these two lots?
  4. Test analyst: Comparable test conditions, product configuration, and bin definitions, plus the relevant lot history.
  5. Product engineer: Those checks are pending. I should not treat the lower bin as proof of a packaging defect.
  6. Test analyst: Correct. A bin records classification under the test criteria; attribution needs additional evidence.
  7. Product engineer: Can we still flag the distribution for the package and test teams to review jointly?
  8. Test analyst: Yes. Report the observed counts and preserve the unverified conditions as explicit questions.
  9. Product engineer: I'll avoid calling the lot unqualified solely from this comparison without the program's review.
  10. Test analyst: I'll bring the bin definitions and available records so the responsible team can assess the finding.

Pending is neither passed nor failed

A fictional package plan requires tests A, B, and C plus final review. A passed, B is running, and C has not started. No substitution or final approval is recorded.

Choose one reply for each gap, then read the four turns in order. Check the explanation after each choice.

1. Engineer: "Keep A's passing result as test ___, not a claim that every requirement is complete."

Answer and explanation

B. evidence

The passing result is evidence for its defined test, not completion of the whole plan.

2. Reviewer: "B and C are still required by the approved ___."

Answer and explanation

B. plan

The approved qualification plan still requires these tests; neither has an accepted replacement.

3. Engineer: "We would need an accepted technical ___ before substituting related results."

Answer and explanation

D. rationale

A justified and accepted rationale is necessary for a relevant substitution; none exists here.

4. Reviewer: "Until the tests and final review are complete, do not announce qualification ___."

Answer and explanation

A. approval

Qualification approval remains pending while required tests and final review are incomplete.

Read the completed exchange twice, switching roles. Keep the printed facts and professional responsibilities unchanged.

Lesson 07: Packaging, Test, and Reliability Qualification
Original fictional case: Product engineer Diego and reliability engineer Mei review package Q7. Its approved fictional qualification plan requires temperature cycling, high-temperature operating life testing, a highly accelerated stress test, and final review of the evidence. Temperature cycling has passed under its protocol. Operating-life testing is running, and the accelerated stress test has not started. No final approval or accepted substitution is recorded. A customer slide nevertheless says qualification complete. The team must replace that headline with a precise status without describing open tests as failures.
Language workshop: One completed test is not complete qualification
Communication goal: Explain qualification status test by test, preserve configuration scope, and correct an overbroad customer claim.
Language guidance: This case uses a specific fictional plan, not a universal mandatory three-test list. One passing test supports its defined result. It does not complete the two open tests or the final review, and it does not establish every application-specific reliability claim.
Useful expressions (preserve the supplied facts): Q7 passed temperature cycling under the stated protocol. / HTOL is still running. / HAST has not started. / The approved plan requires all three tests and final review. / Qualification is in progress, not complete. / No result is available for the unstarted test. / Which package construction does the evidence cover? / Is this the approved qualification vehicle? / Are the required preconditioning records included? / Final test is not a substitute for every reliability stress. / Similarity needs an accepted technical rationale. / A desired customer date does not remove a required test. / Final qualification approval is not recorded. / Identify what each completed test actually addresses. / The next report will distinguish completed, running, and unstarted tests. / Keep release decisions with the authorized review process.
Vocabulary: package substrate: The package structure carrying connections between die and external interfaces. / wire bonding: Forming electrical connections using fine wires. / flip-chip attachment: Connecting a die face-down through conductive bumps or pillars. / underfill: Material placed around interconnections to support a package assembly. / mold compound: Encapsulating material used in many semiconductor packages. / solder joint: A soldered electrical and mechanical connection. / BGA: Ball grid array, a package connection format using an array of solder balls. / QFN: Quad flat no-lead, a package format with exposed connection lands. / SiP: System in package, integrating multiple functions or components in one package. / TSV: Through-silicon via, a conductive connection passing through silicon. / package construction: The materials and structural arrangement of a package. / moisture sensitivity: Susceptibility to moisture-related effects under stated handling or stress conditions. / delamination: Separation between bonded material layers. / thermal cycling: Repeated temperature changes under a specified test profile. / HTOL: High-temperature operating life, an operating stress test under defined conditions. / HAST: Highly accelerated stress test, a defined accelerated humidity-related stress test. / preconditioning: Defined preparation before a test to represent relevant handling or assembly stresses. / qualification plan: The defined tests, evidence, scope, and approval requirements for qualification. / qualification vehicle: The selected device or structure used to support qualification evidence. / test coverage: The requirements or failure concerns addressed by the performed tests. / failure analysis: Investigation of failed samples and their causes. / qualification by similarity: Use of justified related evidence under an accepted qualification approach. / final test: Electrical testing at the defined final product stage. / qualification approval: Authorized acceptance of the required qualification evidence.
Speaking task: Check the answers. Read the three test statuses, expanding HTOL and HAST using the vocabulary pages. Switch roles for turns 9-20. Keep construction, preparation, related evidence, and final approval distinct. Complete and check the transfer. Read the pending work without changing it into either a pass or a failure.
Partner: Diego: Product engineer / Mei: Reliability engineer
Guided response task: Select supplied answers for the dialogue gaps. Check the explanations, then read the completed exchange aloud; no original writing is required.
Optional second-round challenge: A fictional package plan requires tests A, B, and C plus final review. A passed, B is running, and C has not started. No substitution or final approval is recorded.
Model for comparison AFTER my attempt, not a response to give me first: Diego: We also have final electrical test records, but those should not be presented as though they address every stress-related concern in the qualification plan.
Mei: Correct. Test coverage differs between production checks and reliability assessments. Each result needs to be connected to what it actually evaluates, not treated as interchangeable evidence.
Diego: I will change the headline to qualification in progress, list the three statuses, and keep the configuration and outstanding review visible. We will not announce release from this slide.
Mei: That preserves qualification approval as a separate decision. The next update can show genuine progress while keeping the unresolved tests and final review clear.
END REFERENCE

Rehearse with an AI colleague — complete prompt

Copy the full text below into your preferred AI. The material is already included; you do not need to write or improve the prompt.

TASK: Interactive workplace role-play
1. Use the supplied case or dialogue as the starting situation. Give a two-sentence briefing and offer two relevant professional roles for me to choose from. For a supplied dialogue, use its actual roles. Ask which role I want, then stop and wait. Do not write my replies.
2. After I choose, identify who you will play and the immediate communication goal. Play the other professional; where a meeting requires a third person, label each of your speakers clearly. Start with one natural workplace turn and wait for my reply. Keep most turns to one to three sentences and ask no more than one question at a time.
3. Let the exchange develop across six to ten learner turns, or end earlier if I type "feedback". Respond to what I actually say. Include a plausible clarification, disagreement or tradeoff without silently changing the starting facts. Mark any added constraint as a fictional second-round variation. Do not resolve approvals, evidence or commitments that remain uncertain.
4. Stay in role during the exchange. If my meaning is unclear, ask for clarification naturally. Give a hint only if I ask or cannot proceed. Do not deliver a model conversation in advance.
5. At the debrief, quote two of my phrases: one successful choice and one worth improving. Check factual accuracy, language, register and whether the next step was clear. Give up to three focused suggestions. Ask me to retry the weakest turn; wait. Only then offer an alternative wording and a harder replay.
Use voice replies when available. If I prefer selections, offer four plausible spoken replies and explain my choice before continuing. Do not require written compositions.

Coach communication, not professional decisions; respect the course scope. Ask only for fictional or anonymized practice details. Judge clarity, meaning, appropriate tone and the next step. Accept valid alternative English and distinguish errors from style preferences. Do not claim to certify my language level. Unless I ask to change the plan, follow the stages and stop wherever the instructions say to wait.

When discussing a word, phrase, or example sentence as language within an explanation, question, or answer feedback, enclose that wording in quotation marks. For example: What does “about” mean in “about twenty people”? Use “on” with a named day. Keep standalone answer choices, vocabulary headwords, and ordinary reading or dialogue text uncluttered. Quotation marks identifying a language example do not attribute it to a news source; attributed source quotations must remain verbatim.

Practice setting: B2 independent. Use natural professional English with brief explanations. Let me attempt each task without a model first. Offer a hint after difficulty and invite a more precise retry.

REFERENCE
Course: Semiconductor English
Professional audience: semiconductor process engineers, yield engineers, product engineers, equipment engineers, fab supervisors, quality teams, test and packaging teams, foundry coordinators, supply planners, applications engineers, and technical program managers
Scope: Original fictional English practice, not a fabrication recipe, equipment procedure, product qualification, design sign-off, or production authorization. Numbers, lots, organizations, and schedules are invented. Real work must follow approved process documents, safety rules, applicable standards, customer requirements, and authorized engineering decisions.
Lesson 07: Packaging, Test, and Reliability Qualification
Original fictional case: Product engineer Diego and reliability engineer Mei review package Q7. Its approved fictional qualification plan requires temperature cycling, high-temperature operating life testing, a highly accelerated stress test, and final review of the evidence. Temperature cycling has passed under its protocol. Operating-life testing is running, and the accelerated stress test has not started. No final approval or accepted substitution is recorded. A customer slide nevertheless says qualification complete. The team must replace that headline with a precise status without describing open tests as failures.
Language workshop: One completed test is not complete qualification
Communication goal: Explain qualification status test by test, preserve configuration scope, and correct an overbroad customer claim.
Language guidance: This case uses a specific fictional plan, not a universal mandatory three-test list. One passing test supports its defined result. It does not complete the two open tests or the final review, and it does not establish every application-specific reliability claim.
Useful expressions (preserve the supplied facts): Q7 passed temperature cycling under the stated protocol. / HTOL is still running. / HAST has not started. / The approved plan requires all three tests and final review. / Qualification is in progress, not complete. / No result is available for the unstarted test. / Which package construction does the evidence cover? / Is this the approved qualification vehicle? / Are the required preconditioning records included? / Final test is not a substitute for every reliability stress. / Similarity needs an accepted technical rationale. / A desired customer date does not remove a required test. / Final qualification approval is not recorded. / Identify what each completed test actually addresses. / The next report will distinguish completed, running, and unstarted tests. / Keep release decisions with the authorized review process.
Vocabulary: package substrate: The package structure carrying connections between die and external interfaces. / wire bonding: Forming electrical connections using fine wires. / flip-chip attachment: Connecting a die face-down through conductive bumps or pillars. / underfill: Material placed around interconnections to support a package assembly. / mold compound: Encapsulating material used in many semiconductor packages. / solder joint: A soldered electrical and mechanical connection. / BGA: Ball grid array, a package connection format using an array of solder balls. / QFN: Quad flat no-lead, a package format with exposed connection lands. / SiP: System in package, integrating multiple functions or components in one package. / TSV: Through-silicon via, a conductive connection passing through silicon. / package construction: The materials and structural arrangement of a package. / moisture sensitivity: Susceptibility to moisture-related effects under stated handling or stress conditions. / delamination: Separation between bonded material layers. / thermal cycling: Repeated temperature changes under a specified test profile. / HTOL: High-temperature operating life, an operating stress test under defined conditions. / HAST: Highly accelerated stress test, a defined accelerated humidity-related stress test. / preconditioning: Defined preparation before a test to represent relevant handling or assembly stresses. / qualification plan: The defined tests, evidence, scope, and approval requirements for qualification. / qualification vehicle: The selected device or structure used to support qualification evidence. / test coverage: The requirements or failure concerns addressed by the performed tests. / failure analysis: Investigation of failed samples and their causes. / qualification by similarity: Use of justified related evidence under an accepted qualification approach. / final test: Electrical testing at the defined final product stage. / qualification approval: Authorized acceptance of the required qualification evidence.
Speaking task: Check the answers. Read the three test statuses, expanding HTOL and HAST using the vocabulary pages. Switch roles for turns 9-20. Keep construction, preparation, related evidence, and final approval distinct. Complete and check the transfer. Read the pending work without changing it into either a pass or a failure.
Partner: Diego: Product engineer / Mei: Reliability engineer
Guided response task: Select supplied answers for the dialogue gaps. Check the explanations, then read the completed exchange aloud; no original writing is required.
Optional second-round challenge: A fictional package plan requires tests A, B, and C plus final review. A passed, B is running, and C has not started. No substitution or final approval is recorded.
Model for comparison AFTER my attempt, not a response to give me first: Diego: We also have final electrical test records, but those should not be presented as though they address every stress-related concern in the qualification plan.
Mei: Correct. Test coverage differs between production checks and reliability assessments. Each result needs to be connected to what it actually evaluates, not treated as interchangeable evidence.
Diego: I will change the headline to qualification in progress, list the three statuses, and keep the configuration and outstanding review visible. We will not announce release from this slide.
Mei: That preserves qualification approval as a separate decision. The next update can show genuine progress while keeping the unresolved tests and final review clear.
END REFERENCE
08Foundry, Tape-Out, PDK, and Capacity CommunicationA possible slot is not tape-out readiness+

Your goal

Negotiate a requested date by separating design sign-off, data delivery, foundry acceptance, and capacity confirmation.

This lesson in the book, page 67 ↗

A Read the situation

A possible slot is not tape-out readiness

Customer design lead Sofia asks foundry liaison Ken to move a planned October 15 tape-out to October 8. Four design-rule-check findings and one layout-versus-schematic mismatch remain unresolved in the agreed fictional PDK revision P3. The foundry has mentioned a possible earlier slot but has not reserved or accepted it. No complete sign-off package is available, and no waiver is approved. Ken must communicate the blockers and conditional next steps without promising a wafer start, finished samples, or shipment.

Sofia: Customer design lead / Ken: Foundry liaison

Check the facts · 3 questions

Choose the answer supported by the briefing. Do not assume that a proposed action has already happened.

1. Which earlier date is requested?

Answer and explanation

B. October 8 tape-out

Sofia asks to move tape-out from October 15 to October 8, not to deliver finished devices then.

2. What remains unresolved in the design checks?

Answer and explanation

B. Four DRC findings and one LVS mismatch

The briefing explicitly lists four design-rule findings and one layout-versus-schematic mismatch.

3. What is the capacity status?

Answer and explanation

D. A possible earlier slot, not reserved or accepted

A mentioned opportunity is not a recorded capacity commitment or approval.

B Find the words

Vocabulary and collocations

October 8 is a requested tape-out date, not an accepted slot or a finished-sample date. The open DRC and LVS items remain blockers to the stated sign-off package. The case does not provide an approved waiver or permission to bypass checks.

24 field terms and natural word combinations
foundry
A manufacturer producing semiconductor devices for other companies.coordinate with the foundry
fabless company
A chip-design company that contracts out fabrication.support a fabless customer
IDM
Integrated device manufacturer, combining chip design and manufacturing.work with an IDM
PDK
Process design kit: process-specific models, rules, and design resources.confirm the PDK revision
design rule
A process-specific constraint governing layout features or relationships.check design rules
DRC
Design rule checking, testing layout against applicable rule definitions.resolve DRC findings
LVS
Layout versus schematic checking, comparing extracted layout connectivity with the schematic.close an LVS mismatch
rule deck
The implemented rules used by a physical-verification tool.identify the rule deck
sign-off
The required formal completion and approval of defined checks.complete design sign-off
tape-out
Release of the approved design dataset for the intended fabrication handoff.plan the tape-out
GDSII
A widely used layout-data format for integrated circuit design.deliver a GDSII dataset
OASIS
A compact integrated-circuit layout interchange format.verify the OASIS file
mask data preparation
Processing layout data for mask manufacture.schedule mask data preparation
mask set
The collection of masks needed for a defined fabrication flow.release the mask set
engineering change order
A controlled record authorizing a defined engineering change, abbreviated ECO.approve an engineering change order
waiver
An authorized exception to a specific requirement under an applicable process.request a defined waiver
data acceptance
Confirmation that a delivered dataset meets the receiving process's requirements.obtain foundry data acceptance
capacity reservation
A confirmed allocation of manufacturing capacity.confirm capacity reservation
wafer start
Entry of a wafer lot into the defined fabrication flow.confirm the wafer start
cycle time
Elapsed time through a defined manufacturing flow or stage.state fabrication cycle time
engineering lot
A lot used for development or engineering evaluation.plan an engineering lot
risk production
Production begun before all defined qualification or maturity conditions are complete.assess risk-production approval
respin
A revised design iteration requiring another fabrication cycle.evaluate the need for a respin
delivery commitment
An agreed promise about a specified deliverable and date.qualify the delivery commitment

PDK and rule-deck versions affect what physical verification means. Keep results connected to the agreed revision. A clean check run also has a defined scope; it does not guarantee first-silicon performance, complete qualification, or a confirmed manufacturing schedule.

C Notice the language

Separate the milestones under date pressure

Tape-out, foundry data acceptance, wafer start, and finished samples are related but distinct milestones. State which date is requested and which prerequisites remain open. A possible capacity opportunity should trigger a feasibility discussion, not erase design checks or become a shipment promise.

16 useful phrases, grouped by purpose
Name the requested milestone
You are requesting October 8 tape-out.
Separate later dates
That is not a wafer-start or sample-delivery commitment.
State the open checks
Four DRC findings and one LVS mismatch remain open.
Confirm the basis
The checks use the agreed PDK revision P3.
Avoid silent version changes
Keep the rule deck and design dataset identified.
Qualify the slot
The foundry mentioned a possibility, not a reservation.
Ask about acceptance
What is required for the foundry to accept the dataset?
Keep sign-off visible
The complete sign-off package is not yet available.
Bound the exception
No waiver is approved for these findings.
Preserve the decision route
Any exception must follow the applicable authorization process.
Request a feasible sequence
Align check closure, data review, and capacity confirmation.
Avoid a downstream promise
We cannot infer finished samples from a tape-out target.
Clarify ownership
Who owns each open check and the next status update?
Record the dependency
The earlier request depends on both technical readiness and capacity.
State the next update
We will report check status and slot confirmation separately.
Close conditionally
October 8 remains a request pending the required evidence and acceptance.
6 language and precision notes
Slot
Clarify whether possible, held, reserved, or confirmed.
Ready
Identify which handoff and its required checks.
Tape-out
Not interchangeable with wafer start or finished-device delivery.
Clean
State the check scope, version, and remaining exceptions.
Waived
Requires an actual authorized exception, not a schedule preference.
Committed
Name the deliverable, date, dependencies, and accepting party.

D Check your understanding

Choose the precise message

Choose one best answer using the case facts and the stated purpose.

1. Which reply to the earlier-date request is supported?

Answer and explanation

A. October 8 remains conditional on check closure, the required handoff, and capacity confirmation.

The reply preserves the separate technical and capacity prerequisites without inventing acceptance.

2. What does an LVS mismatch concern?

Answer and explanation

A. A difference between extracted layout connectivity and the schematic

LVS compares the layout-derived circuit with the schematic. Spacing rules, timing slack, and overlay belong to different verification or measurement questions.

3. Why retain the PDK and rule-deck versions with results?

Answer and explanation

B. The check result depends on the process-specific definitions actually used.

Traceable versions identify the actual basis of the result. A filename is insufficient, and neither a later release nor an earlier clean run establishes unchanged applicability.

4. Which statement about tape-out is accurate?

Answer and explanation

C. It is a design-data handoff milestone, not proof of wafer start or sample availability.

Fabrication, test, qualification, and delivery remain distinct activities after the design-data handoff.

Answers and explanations
  1. tape-out Turn 2. Tape-out is the design-data release milestone being requested, not a confirmed wafer start or finished-sample date.
  2. sign-off Turn 4. Sign-off is the required completion and approval of the defined checks; the complete package is not yet available here.
  3. PDK Turn 6. The PDK supplies process-specific design resources; its agreed revision must remain connected to the verification results.
  4. DRC Turn 8. DRC checks the layout against applicable design rules; its open findings need documented resolution rather than a changed headline.
  5. LVS Turn 10. LVS compares extracted layout connectivity with the schematic and therefore addresses a different verification question from geometric rule checks.
  6. capacity reservation Turn 12. Capacity reservation is an actual allocation; a possible earlier slot has not been reserved or accepted in this case.
  7. Data acceptance Turn 14. Data acceptance confirms the receiving process's requirements have been met; transmitting files alone does not establish it.
  8. waiver Turn 16. A waiver is an authorized exception to a specific requirement; none is approved for the open findings here.
  9. wafer start Turn 18. A wafer start is the lot's entry into fabrication and is distinct from the earlier design-data handoff milestone.
  10. delivery commitment Turn 20. A delivery commitment must identify an accepted deliverable and date; neither a requested tape-out nor a possible slot guarantees finished samples.

Three more conversations at work

Each short conversation has its own fictional situation and facts.

An earlier tape-out slot remains conditional

Fictional foundry negotiation using the lesson case: a customer requests an earlier tape-out slot, design checks are open, and capacity is limited.

  1. Customer program manager: Can the foundry move our tape-out earlier? The project team wants a firmer customer date.
  2. Foundry liaison: We can discuss options, but design checks remain open and capacity allocation is limited.
  3. Customer program manager: Could you reserve the earlier slot now and assume the checks will finish in time?
  4. Foundry liaison: I can't promise that. We need the design-readiness position and the foundry's actual allocation decision.
  5. Customer program manager: What can you offer today that helps us plan without creating a false commitment?
  6. Foundry liaison: I can request available options and state the readiness conditions attached to each proposal.
  7. Customer program manager: Please include the required process design kit, or PDK, version in that readiness discussion.
  8. Foundry liaison: Yes. The design team should confirm its check basis rather than assume versions are interchangeable.
  9. Customer program manager: I'll report the earlier date as requested, not secured, until those conditions and capacity are confirmed.
  10. Foundry liaison: I'll return with the foundry response and keep any unresolved checks explicit in the negotiation.
A new PDK version before submission

Fictional design handoff: a team has checks against PDK version 6, while a proposed slot refers to version 7; applicability is unconfirmed.

  1. Design manager: Our checks passed against PDK six. Can we accept the proposed slot referring to PDK seven?
  2. Foundry interface engineer: First we need to confirm the applicable submission requirements and the effect of that version difference.
  3. Design manager: Could we simply rename the package so it matches the newer version in the slot note?
  4. Foundry interface engineer: No. A label change would not establish that the design was checked against the required basis.
  5. Design manager: Then what conditional proposal can we take back while preserving the current completed work?
  6. Foundry interface engineer: Ask whether the existing basis is acceptable or what reviewed updates are needed before submission.
  7. Design manager: I'll have the design-check owner assess that question without promising an immediate rerun completion.
  8. Foundry interface engineer: I'll clarify the foundry's slot conditions and whether timing alternatives are available.
  9. Design manager: Until then, our tape-out date remains provisional, with the version question clearly stated.
  10. Foundry interface engineer: Agreed. We'll negotiate from verified readiness and capacity information, not from a renamed file.
Splitting a request does not create capacity

Fictional capacity discussion: a customer proposes splitting one manufacturing request into two smaller requests; available foundry capacity has not been confirmed.

  1. Customer planner: Could we split our request into two smaller allocations and secure an earlier start that way?
  2. Foundry account lead: We can ask about phased allocation, but splitting the request doesn't itself create available capacity.
  3. Customer planner: I understand. The design team would still need to meet the same agreed readiness conditions.
  4. Foundry account lead: Yes, and the foundry must confirm whether the proposed phasing fits its actual planning constraints.
  5. Customer planner: Could you present the phased option alongside the original request without canceling the original proposal?
  6. Foundry account lead: I'll clarify how alternatives should be submitted so we don't unintentionally create duplicate commitments.
  7. Customer planner: What should I tell our internal team about timing while that discussion is ongoing?
  8. Foundry account lead: Say phased capacity is under discussion, with no earlier slot confirmed and readiness still subject to review.
  9. Customer planner: I'll keep both options conditional and ask the design owner for an updated check status.
  10. Foundry account lead: I'll bring back the capacity response so we can compare workable choices rather than assumed dates.

A requested handoff is not a shipment

A team requests tape-out on November 3. Two DRC items remain open. The foundry has mentioned a possible slot but has not reserved it. No waiver or sample-delivery date is approved.

Choose one reply for each gap, then read the four turns in order. Check the explanation after each choice.

1. Designer: "Keep November third attached to the requested design-data handoff: ___."

Answer and explanation

A. tape-out

Tape-out identifies the requested design-data handoff, not a later manufacturing or delivery event.

2. Liaison: "The possible slot is not yet an allocated ___."

Answer and explanation

A. capacity reservation

Capacity reservation requires a confirmed allocation; a possible slot has not reached that status.

3. Designer: "I will not tell the customer that fabrication begins then; we have no confirmed ___."

Answer and explanation

C. wafer start

A wafer start is distinct from the requested design-data handoff and is not confirmed here.

4. Liaison: "And discussing a slot does not establish a finished-sample ___."

Answer and explanation

D. delivery commitment

A delivery commitment needs an accepted deliverable and date, neither of which follows from discussing a slot.

Vocabulary: foundry: A manufacturer producing semiconductor devices for other companies. / fabless company: A chip-design company that contracts out fabrication. / IDM: Integrated device manufacturer, combining chip design and manufacturing. / PDK: Process design kit: process-specific models, rules, and design resources. / design rule: A process-specific constraint governing layout features or relationships. / DRC: Design rule checking, testing layout against applicable rule definitions. / LVS: Layout versus schematic checking, comparing extracted layout connectivity with the schematic. / rule deck: The implemented rules used by a physical-verification tool. / sign-off: The required formal completion and approval of defined checks. / tape-out: Release of the approved design dataset for the intended fabrication handoff. / GDSII: A widely used layout-data format for integrated circuit design. / OASIS: A compact integrated-circuit layout interchange format. / mask data preparation: Processing layout data for mask manufacture. / mask set: The collection of masks needed for a defined fabrication flow. / engineering change order: A controlled record authorizing a defined engineering change, abbreviated ECO. / waiver: An authorized exception to a specific requirement under an applicable process. / data acceptance: Confirmation that a delivered dataset meets the receiving process's requirements. / capacity reservation: A confirmed allocation of manufacturing capacity. / wafer start: Entry of a wafer lot into the defined fabrication flow. / cycle time: Elapsed time through a defined manufacturing flow or stage. / engineering lot: A lot used for development or engineering evaluation. / risk production: Production begun before all defined qualification or maturity conditions are complete. / respin: A revised design iteration requiring another fabrication cycle. / delivery commitment: An agreed promise about a specified deliverable and date.
